Lecture 17

Sure and almost sure convergence, the SLLN and the sample mean

Deck B, slides 11 to 19 · 43 min read · 11 practice problems

Solutions stay collapsed until you click them.

Big picture. L16 ended with a question: what should "Xn​→X" mean when every Xn​ is random? For numbers and for functions we already know what convergence means. The trick of this lecture is to reuse that knowledge, by remembering one fact from L1:

A random variable is just a function X:Ω→R. The randomness is all in which outcome ω nature picks.

So once nature picks ω, the whole sequence X1​(ω),X2​(ω),X3​(ω),… is an ordinary sequence of numbers, and we can ask whether it converges. This lecture gives the two answers that work outcome by outcome:

  • Sure convergence: the sequence of numbers converges to X(ω) for every outcome ω.
  • Almost sure convergence: it converges for all outcomes except a set of probability 0.

Then come three things built on these ideas:

  1. The headline example, the strong law of large numbers (SLLN). It is the theorem behind Monte Carlo (L15) and behind using the sample mean as an estimator.
  2. The main tool for proving almost sure convergence, the Borel–Cantelli criterion.
  3. A warning: almost sure convergence does not force the means E[Xn​] to converge.

A picture worth keeping in mind for the whole lecture: think of each ω as one "universe" or one run of an experiment. Each universe produces its own path n↦Xn​(ω). Sure convergence asks every path to converge. Almost sure convergence lets a few paths misbehave, as long as together those paths carry no probability.

Part A: the slides

Slide 11/30: Recap

On the slide. Convergence of Xn​→X. X could even be a deterministic number. The Xn​'s could be dependent on each other. Each Xn​ could have a different law (pmf/pdf).

This repeats the last slide of L16 (see the examples there). The three bullets are warnings about how general the setting is:

  • The limit may be a constant. Most famous limits are constants: the SLLN limit is the number μ. A constant c is still a random variable, namely the function X(ω)=c for every ω.
  • The Xn​ may be dependent. In fact they usually are. For example μ^​n​ and μ^​n+1​ share n of their data points. So no theorem in this lecture may quietly assume independence unless it says so.
  • The laws may change with n. For example Xn​∼N(0,n1​) gets narrower with n.

One thing is not allowed to vary: all the Xn​ and X live on the same sample space Ω. Without that, "Xn​(ω) versus X(ω)" would make no sense. (L18's convergence in distribution is the one mode that drops this requirement.)

Slide 12/30: Pointwise or sure convergence

On the slide. {Xn​,n≥0} converges to X pointwise or surely if for all ω∈Ω we have limn→∞​Xn​(ω)=X(ω). Example: Ω={H,T},

Xn​={n1​1+n1​​if ω=Hif ω=T​andX={01​if ω=Hif ω=T.​

The idea. This is slide 8 of L16 (pointwise convergence of functions) applied to the functions Xn​:Ω→R. Fix an outcome, look at the sequence of numbers it produces, and check that it converges to the right number. Do this for every outcome.

Written with ϵ and N, as in L16:

for every ω∈Ω and every ϵ>0, there is N(ϵ,ω) with ∣Xn​(ω)−X(ω)∣<ϵ for all n>N(ϵ,ω).

The N is allowed to depend on ω, exactly as in pointwise convergence of functions.

Probability plays no role. Notice that P does not appear anywhere in the definition. It is a statement about functions only. That is the reason for the name "sure": no matter what happens, the sequence converges.

The example. One coin toss decides everything, and there are only two outcomes, so we can check both by hand.

  • If ω=H: the realized sequence is 1,21​,31​,…, which tends to 0=X(H). ✓
  • If ω=T: the realized sequence is 2,23​,34​,…, which tends to 1=X(T). ✓

Every outcome gives a sequence converging to the right limit, so Xn​→X surely.

Even uniform. Here ∣Xn​(ω)−X(ω)∣=n1​ for both outcomes, so the same N=ϵ1​ works for every ω. The convergence is uniform on Ω (L16 slide 9).

Note the structure. Xn​=X+n1​. The randomness is decided once, by the toss, and after that the sequence slides deterministically towards X. Whether the coin is fair, or lands heads with probability 0.999, changes nothing. This is a second way to see that sure convergence ignores probabilities.

Slide 13/30: Almost sure convergence

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X almost surely if P(ω∈Ω:limn→∞​Xn​(ω)=X(ω))=1. The set of outcomes where convergence does not happen has measure 0: P{ω∈Ω:limn​Xn​(ω)=X(ω)}=0. Example: Ω=[0,1], pick a number uniformly in [0,1]. Let Xn​(ω)=ωn and X(ω)=0 for all ω. Xn​(ω)→X(ω) for ω∈[0,1). Xn​(ω)→X(ω) for ω=1, and P{ω=1} [=0]. This is almost sure convergence as P{[0,1)}=1.

(The slide's line "and P{ω=1}" is missing "=0".)

Why we need something weaker than sure. Sure convergence is too strict for probability. A single strange outcome, one that will essentially never occur, can ruin it. Almost sure convergence says: let such outcomes misbehave, as long as their total probability is zero.

Reading the definition. Collect all the "lucky" outcomes, the ones whose path converges to the right limit, into one event:

C={ω:Xn​(ω)→X(ω)}.

Then

Xn​a.s.​X⟺P(C)=1⟺P(Cc)=0​

Unlucky outcomes (Cc) may exist. They just carry no probability. Other names and notation: Xn​→X with probability 1 (w.p.1), or a.s.

The example, step by step. This is the function xn from L16 slide 8, now viewed as a random variable: nature picks ω uniformly in [0,1], and Xn​(ω)=ωn.

  • If ω∈[0,1): ωn→0, because a number of size less than 1 shrinks geometrically when you keep multiplying it by itself. For example ω=0.9 gives 0.9,0.81,0.729,⋯→0. These outcomes are lucky.
  • If ω=1: 1n=1 for every n, which does not tend to 0. This outcome is unlucky.
  • So C=[0,1). Under the uniform distribution a single point has probability 0, so P(C)=1−P({1})=1−0=1.

Hence Xn​a.s.​0. But Xn​ does not converge to 0 surely, because of the single outcome ω=1.

Sure versus almost sure.

  • Sure ⇒ almost sure. If every outcome is lucky then C=Ω, and P(Ω)=1.
  • Almost sure ⇒ sure. The example above.

In probability, almost sure is the natural notion. Changing random variables on an event of probability 0 changes no probability, no expectation and no distribution, so a theory that cared about such events would be caring about something invisible. That is why sure convergence is rarely used after this slide.

A useful equivalent form (needed on slide 18). What does "the path converges" mean for one ω? By the ϵ–N definition: for every ϵ>0, the path is within ϵ of X(ω) from some time on. So

Xn​a.s.​X⟺with probability 1, for every ϵ>0, ∣Xn​−X∣<ϵ for all large enough n.

Turn it around and look at the bad events En​(ϵ)={∣Xn​−X∣≥ϵ}. "Within ϵ for all large n" means "only finitely many En​(ϵ) happen". So, equivalently,

Xn​a.s.​X⟺for each ϵ>0,P(En​(ϵ) happens for infinitely many n)=0.

(The step "for every ϵ" can be moved outside the probability because it is enough to check the countably many values ϵ=1,21​,31​,…, and a countable union of probability-0 events still has probability 0. Slide 18 uses exactly this.)

So almost sure convergence is about the whole tail of the path: deviations of size ϵ must eventually stop for good. Keep this in mind, because L18's convergence in probability only asks that deviations become rare at each fixed time, which is weaker.

Slide 14/30: Example 2, the strong law of large numbers

On the slide. Let {Xn​,n≥0} be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with mean μ and Sn​=∑i=1n​Xi​. Then nSn​​→μ a.s. Toss a biased coin (probability of heads μ) repeatedly. What is ω and Ω? Let Xi​ be the outcome of the i-th toss and Sn​ the number of heads in n tosses. The empirical mean is nSn​​.

X1​,X2​,… i.i.d., E∣X1​∣<∞, μ=E[X1​]⟹μ^​n​=nSn​​a.s.​μ​

In words. Average more and more i.i.d. copies of a random quantity, and the running average settles down to the true mean, along essentially every possible run of the experiment.

The exact hypothesis. The mean must exist and be finite, E∣X1​∣<∞. No finite variance is needed for the theorem (the short proof in B12 below assumes more, which makes the proof easier, not the theorem truer).

What is ω and Ω? (the blue question). This question is the heart of the slide. The SLLN talks about the limit of nSn​​ as n→∞, so it is a statement about the whole infinite sequence of tosses. An outcome must therefore record all of them, not just one toss.

  • An outcome ω is one infinite sequence of tosses, for example ω=(H,T,T,H,H,…).
  • The sample space is the set of all such sequences:
Ω={H,T}N={(ω1​,ω2​,…):ωi​∈{H,T}}.

This set is uncountable (like the binary expansions of numbers in [0,1]).

  • The random variables just read off coordinates: Xi​(ω)=1 if ωi​=H, and 0 otherwise. Then Sn​(ω) is the number of H's among the first n coordinates, and nSn​(ω)​ is the fraction of heads so far.

With this set-up, the SLLN says precisely

P({ω:nSn​(ω)​→μ})=1.

That is the definition of slide 13, with Xn​ replaced by nSn​​ and X by the constant μ.

The unlucky outcomes. They really exist.

  • ω=(H,H,H,…) has nSn​​=1 for every n. So it is unlucky whenever μ<1.
  • The block sequence from L16 (blocks of H's and T's whose lengths keep doubling) makes nSn​​ swing up and down forever, so it has no limit at all.

In fact there are uncountably many unlucky sequences, and yet their total probability is 0.

"Probability 0" does not mean "impossible". For 0<μ<1, every single sequence has probability 0. Reason: the probability that the first n tosses match a given pattern is a product of n factors, each at most max(μ,1−μ)<1, so it is at most max(μ,1−μ)n→0. So the all-heads sequence is no "less possible" than any other single sequence. What the SLLN says is that the set of sequences with the wrong frequency of heads is negligible.

Why the SLLN matters in this course.

  • Monte Carlo (L15 slide 17). The values g(U1​),g(U2​),… are i.i.d. with finite mean θ=∫01​g. So their average converges to θ with probability 1. This is why Monte Carlo works.
  • Probability as long-run frequency. Take Xi​=1{A happens on trial i}. Then E[Xi​]=P(A), and the fraction of trials on which A happens converges to P(A) almost surely. The intuitive "frequency" meaning of probability becomes a theorem.
  • The sample mean as an estimator (slide 15).

When it fails. Without a finite mean the SLLN can fail. For i.i.d. standard Cauchy samples, nSn​​ is again standard Cauchy for every n (a known property of the Cauchy distribution). Averaging does not shrink the spread at all, so the running mean never settles down. This is the simulation of L15 Part B, B10.

Slide 15/30: Detour, the sample mean as an estimator

On the slide. Now that we know nSn​​→μ, we can use μ^​n​:=nSn​​ as an "estimator" for the mean, especially when the underlying distribution is not known. The estimator μ^​n​ is a random variable. What is its CDF? What are its mean and variance? μ^​n​ is an "unbiased estimator" since E[μ^​n​]=μ. Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​. We will soon see the CLT, which will tell us the CDF of μ^​n​ without any information on the law of the Xi​.

The set-up. You do not know the distribution of the data, and you want its mean μ. The SLLN suggests the obvious recipe: average your data. The slide calls μ^​n​ an estimator, a formula that turns data into a guess. (L21 develops estimators properly.)

The estimator is random. Each data set gives one number μ^​n​(ω). Collect a fresh data set and you get a different number. So μ^​n​ is a random variable, and it makes sense to ask about its mean, its variance and its distribution. These describe how good the recipe is before you see the data.

Its mean. Use linearity of expectation. Note that this step needs no independence at all:

E[μ^​n​]=E[n1​i=1∑n​Xi​]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Xi​]=n1​⋅nμ=μ.

An estimator whose expected value equals the quantity it estimates is called unbiased. It may be off on any particular data set, but it is right on average: it does not systematically over- or under-shoot.

Its variance. Two steps. First pull out the constant n1​ using Var(aY)=a2Var(Y); it comes out squared. Then use independence: variances of independent variables add (toolkit fact 5), and each Xi​ has variance σ2.

Var(μ^​n​)=n21​Var(i=1∑n​Xi​)=n21​⋅nσ2=nσ2​.

(Here we do need independence, or at least that the Xi​ are uncorrelated. Without it, covariance terms would appear.)

E[μ^​n​]=μ,Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​,SD(μ^​n​)=n​σ​​

Reading the result. The estimator is centred on the truth, and its spread shrinks like n​σ​, called the standard error. Because of the square root, accuracy is expensive: to halve the typical error you need four times as much data, and for one more correct decimal digit you need a hundred times as much.

Example. A coin with P(H)=μ has σ2=μ(1−μ)≤41​. With n=10,000 tosses, SD(μ^​n​)≤1001/2​=0.005. So the observed fraction of heads is typically within about half a percentage point of μ.

What is its CDF? The exact answer depends on the law of the Xi​, and it is known only in special cases. These come from the MGF results of L14, since Sn​=nμ^​n​ is a sum of i.i.d. variables:

Xi​ distribution of Sn​=nμ^​n​ (from)
Bernoulli(p) Binomial(n,p) L14 slide 6
Poisson(λ) Poisson(nλ) L14 slide 5
Exp(λ) Gamma(n,λ) L14 slide 6
N(μ,σ2) N(nμ,nσ2) L14 slide 5

For a general distribution there is no closed form. The CLT (L18) gives the approximate answer in every case, which is what the slide promises:

μ^​n​≈N(μ,nσ2​)for large n.

Notice that the mean and variance in this approximation are exactly the ones we just computed.

Slide 16/30: Detour, the incremental formula for the sample mean

On the slide. Given μ^​n​, suppose you see an additional sample Xn+1​. How will you compute μ^​n+1​? Naive way: μ^​n+1​=n+1∑i=1n+1​Xi​​. There is an incremental formula that uses μ^​n​:

μ^​n+1​=μ^​n​+n+11​[Xn+1​−μ^​n​].

Such averaging formulas are used extensively in reinforcement learning.

The question. Data arrives one point at a time (a sensor, a game being played, a website's visitors). You want the current average after every new point. Do you have to add everything up again each time?

Derivation. No. The old mean already "remembers" the old sum, because Sn​=nμ^​n​. So:

  1. The new sum is the old sum plus the new point: Sn+1​=Sn​+Xn+1​=nμ^​n​+Xn+1​.
  2. Divide by n+1, and write nμ^​n​ as (n+1)μ^​n​−μ^​n​ so that a whole μ^​n​ splits off:
μ^​n+1​=n+1nμ^​n​+Xn+1​​=n+1(n+1)μ^​n​−μ^​n​+Xn+1​​=μ^​n​+n+11​(Xn+1​−μ^​n​).
μ^​n+1​=μ^​n​+n+11​(Xn+1​−μ^​n​)​

Reading it.

new estimate=old estimate+step size×(new observation−old estimate).
  • The bracket Xn+1​−μ^​n​ is the surprise: how far the new data point is from what you expected.
  • The estimate moves a fraction n+11​ of the way towards the new point. If the point is above the current mean, the mean goes up, and vice versa.
  • As n grows the steps shrink. One extra data point barely moves an average of a million points. So the estimate settles down, consistent with the SLLN.

Why it is useful. The naive way stores all the data and costs O(n) work per update. The incremental way stores two numbers (μ^​n​ and n) and costs O(1) per update.

The reinforcement-learning connection. In RL, value estimates are updated as

Q←Q+α(target−Q).

With α=n+11​ this is exactly the running mean. With a constant α (say 0.1) every old observation's weight gets multiplied by 1−α at each step, so the estimate becomes an exponentially weighted average. It forgets old data, which is what you want when the environment changes over time.

Quick example. Data 4,8,6,10:

  • μ^​1​=4 (the first point).
  • μ^​2​=4+21​(8−4)=6.
  • μ^​3​=6+31​(6−6)=6. The new point equals the mean, so there is no surprise and no change.
  • μ^​4​=6+41​(10−6)=7.

Check: 44+8+6+10​=7. ✓

Slide 17/30: Recap, modes of convergence

On the slide. Sure convergence (box). Almost sure convergence (box). SLLN: {Xn​} i.i.d. with mean μ and Sn​=∑Xi​; then μ^​n​:=nSn​​→μ a.s. The estimator μ^​n​ has mean μ and variance nσ2​. μ^​n+1​=μ^​n​+n+11​[Xn+1​−μ^​n​].

Nothing new on this slide. The summary so far:

  • Sure = every path converges. Almost sure = the paths that fail have probability 0. Sure ⇒ almost sure, not conversely.
  • The SLLN is an almost sure statement about the sample mean.
  • The sample mean is unbiased with variance nσ2​, and it can be updated in O(1) time.

Slide 18/30: The Borel–Cantelli lemma

On the slide. Self-study: Theorem 7.5 (probabilitycourse.com). Consider a sequence of random variables X1​,X2​,…. If for all ϵ we have ∑n=1∞​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)<∞, then Xn​→X a.s. This is only a sufficient condition for almost sure convergence! Thm 7.6 (HW) gives necessary and sufficient conditions. Lots of problems in probabilitycourse; practice them!

The problem it solves. Checking almost sure convergence straight from the definition means finding the set C of lucky outcomes and computing its probability. That is easy when Ω=[0,1] and the formula is explicit (slide 13), but usually it is hopeless. Theorem 7.5 replaces it with something you can compute: the probabilities P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ) at each single time n.

n=1∑∞​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)<∞  for every ϵ>0⟹Xn​a.s.​X​

In words. If the chances of an ϵ-sized mistake shrink fast enough to be summable, for every ϵ, then the sequence converges almost surely. Summable means, for example, like n21​, n1.011​ or e−n, but not like n1​.

Intuition. ∑n​P(En​) is the expected number of bad events, because ∑n​P(En​)=E[∑n​1En​​]. If the expected number of mistakes is finite, then the actual number of mistakes is finite with probability 1. Finitely many mistakes means that after the last one, the sequence stays within ϵ for good.

Why it is true (the self-study proof). Fix ϵ and let En​={∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ} be the bad event at time n.

  1. The tail is small. For any starting time m, the union bound (toolkit fact 8) gives
P(n≥m⋃​En​)≤n≥m∑​P(En​).

The right side is the tail of a convergent series, so it goes to 0 as m→∞. 2. "Infinitely often" has probability 0. Suppose En​ happens for infinitely many n. Then whatever m you pick, some En​ with n≥m happens. So the event "En​ infinitely often" is contained in ⋃n≥m​En​ for every m, and

P(En​ infinitely often)≤P(n≥m⋃​En​)for every m.

Let m→∞: by step 1 the right side tends to 0, so the left side is 0. This step on its own is the (first) Borel–Cantelli lemma:

n∑​P(En​)<∞⟹P(En​ infinitely often)=0​

In words: with probability 1, only finitely many of the En​ happen. 3. From one ϵ to all of them. Step 2 says: with probability 1, ∣Xn​−X∣≤ϵ for all large n. Do this for ϵ=1,21​,31​,…. Each value gives an exceptional event of probability 0, and a countable union of probability-0 events has probability 0. So with probability 1, the statement holds for every ϵ=k1​ simultaneously. Since any ϵ>0 is bigger than some k1​, that is exactly Xn​(ω)→X(ω). □

Notice what was not used. Nowhere did we need the Xn​ to be independent. Theorem 7.5 works for any dependence structure. (Contrast the second Borel–Cantelli lemma below.)

Only sufficient. Slide 19's example converges almost surely although ∑n​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=∑n1​=∞. So the condition can fail while the conclusion still holds. A divergent sum tells you nothing on its own.

Theorem 7.6 (the HW): a necessary and sufficient condition. For ϵ>0 define

Am​={∣Xn​−X∣<ϵ for all n≥m},

the event that from time m on, the path stays within ϵ of X forever. Then

Xn​a.s.​X⟺m→∞lim​P(Am​)=1  for every ϵ>0​

Compare with Theorem 7.5: there we looked at one time n at a time. Here Am​ involves the whole future after time m. That is exactly what almost sure convergence is about (slide 13), which is why this condition is both necessary and sufficient.

Proof.

  • The events grow. A1​⊆A2​⊆⋯, because if you stay close from time m on, you certainly stay close from time m+1 on.
  • Their union ⋃m​Am​ is the event "from some time on, always within ϵ", that is, "eventually always within ϵ".
  • Continuity of probability for an increasing sequence of events (toolkit fact 8) gives
m→∞lim​P(Am​)=P(m⋃​Am​)=P(eventually always within ϵ).

(⇒) On the event C where Xn​→X, the path is eventually within ϵ. So C⊆⋃m​Am​, and since P(C)=1, the limit is 1.

(⇐) Suppose the limit is 1 for each ϵ=k1​. Then each event "eventually within k1​" has probability 1. Intersect these countably many probability-1 events; the intersection still has probability 1. On it, for every k the path is eventually within k1​, so it converges. □

How to use Theorem 7.6 in practice. Compute P(Am​), or bound it. This is especially easy when the sequence is monotone or absorbing (once it reaches the limit, it stays there): then Am​ reduces to a single event at time m. See slide 19 and B5.

A companion fact: the second Borel–Cantelli lemma.

En​ independent and n∑​P(En​)=∞⟹P(En​ infinitely often)=1​

In words: if the events are independent and their expected number is infinite, then infinitely many of them really happen. This is the tool for proving that a sequence does not converge almost surely. Independence is essential here; slide 19 shows that without it the conclusion can fail. It is used on slide 20 (L18) and in Part B.

Slide 19/30: Another example of a.s. convergence

On the slide. Consider a uniform random variable U and define Xn​=n1{U≤n1​}​: Xn​=n when U≤n1​ and Xn​=0 otherwise. Given a realization of U, what can you say about the sequence {Xn​}? Once an Xn​ is zero, all higher-indexed variables are also zero! This happens for all realizations other than U=0. In that case, since 0≤n1​ for all n, the Xn​'s run off to infinity and we don't see convergence to 0. But P(U=0)=0. Does E[Xn​]→0? Almost sure convergence does not imply that the means converge!

The key structural point. There is only one random number U, drawn once. Every Xn​ is a function of that same U. So the Xn​ are heavily dependent, and the outcome is ω=U itself.

The realized sequences. Fix U=u and follow the path.

  • If u>0: the condition u≤n1​ means n≤u1​. So Xn​=n for n≤u1​, and Xn​=0 for every n>u1​. The thresholds n1​ shrink, so once n1​ drops below u it stays below, and once Xn​ is 0 it stays 0.
u the path X1​,X2​,X3​,…
0.6 1,0,0,0,…
0.3 1,2,3,0,0,…
0.01 1,2,…,100,0,0,…
0 1,2,3,4,⋯→∞
  • If u=0: 0≤n1​ for every n, so Xn​=n forever and the path runs off to infinity.

The only unlucky outcome is u=0, and P(U=0)=0. So Xn​a.s.​0. (It is not sure convergence, because of u=0.)

The means. Xn​ takes only two values, n and 0, so

E[Xn​]=n⋅P(U≤n1​)+0=n⋅n1​=1for every n.

Hence

E[Xn​]=1→0=E[nlim​Xn​].

Why the means do not follow. Each Xn​ is 0 with probability 1−n1​, but takes the huge value n with the small probability n1​. The product of "huge" and "rare" stays at exactly 1, so the rare big value keeps the mean at 1. This is often called mass escaping to infinity.

Almost sure convergence cannot see this, because it looks at each outcome separately. For each fixed u>0 the big values stop after time u1​. But the outcomes that still have a big value at time n (those with u≤n1​) have a value so large that they keep the average up. Convergence in mean (L18) is the mode that does control this, and it fails here: E∣Xn​−0∣=1→0.

Connection with slide 18.

  • Theorem 7.5 cannot be used. For 0<ϵ<1, P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(U≤n1​)=n1​, and ∑n​n1​=∞. And yet Xn​→0 a.s. This is the counterexample showing Theorem 7.5 is only sufficient.
  • Theorem 7.6 does work. Because the path is absorbed at 0, staying at 0 from time m on is the same as being 0 at time m:
Am​={Xn​=0 for all n≥m}={U>m1​},P(Am​)=1−m1​→1. ✓
  • The second Borel–Cantelli lemma does not apply. The events {U≤n1​} have a divergent sum, but they are nested, not independent. That is exactly why infinitely many of them do not happen.

Coming next. The same formula with independent uniforms Un​ (a fresh one for each n) behaves completely differently. That is the next slide, at the start of L18.

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

How to attack "does Xn​ converge almost surely?" Almost every problem below uses one of four routes. Try them in this order.

  1. Look at the paths directly. If Ω is simple (a coin toss, a uniform U on [0,1]), fix ω, find the path Xn​(ω), and find the set of outcomes where it fails. Is its probability 0?
  2. Theorem 7.5 (summable tails). Compute P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ) and check whether its sum is finite. If yes, you are done, and no independence is needed. If the sum diverges, this route tells you nothing.
  3. Theorem 7.6, or a monotone/absorbing structure. Compute P(Am​). Easy when the path, once at the limit, stays there.
  4. To prove failure: find an event of positive probability on which the path does not converge, or use the second Borel–Cantelli lemma (needs independence).

And for limits built from averages: the SLLN plus "continuous functions of a.s. limits are a.s. limits" (B9).

B1 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 1). A fair coin is tossed once. Xn​=n+1n​ if H, and Xn​=(−1)n if T. Does Xn​ converge almost surely?

Solution

Solution. Route 1: there are only two outcomes, so look at both paths.

  • On H: 21​,32​,43​,⋯→1. Converges.
  • On T: −1,1,−1,1,… oscillates forever. No limit.

So the set of outcomes where the path converges at all is {H}, with P(limXn​=1)=P(H)=21​. For almost sure convergence this set needs probability 1, and 21​<1. So Xn​ does not converge almost surely, to 1 or to anything else.

Takeaway. A failure set is only harmless if it has probability 0. Here the bad outcome T has probability 21​, which is far from negligible.

B2 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 2). Ω=[0,1] with the uniform probability. Xn​(s)=1 if 0≤s<2nn+1​ and 0 otherwise; X(s)=1 if 0≤s<21​ and 0 otherwise. Show Xn​a.s.​X.

Solution

Solution. Route 1. First understand the threshold:

2nn+1​=21​+2n1​,

which decreases to 21​ from above. So Xn​ is the indicator of an interval [0,21​+2n1​) that shrinks down to [0,21​]. Now fix s and split into three cases.

  • s<21​: s is below every threshold, so Xn​(s)=1=X(s) for all n. ✓
  • s>21​: Xn​(s)=0=X(s) as soon as the threshold drops to s or below, that is, 21​+2n1​≤s, which rearranges to n≥2s−11​. After that time it stays 0. ✓
  • s=21​: 21​<21​+2n1​ always, so Xn​(21​)=1 for all n, but X(21​)=0. ✗

The failure set is the single point {21​}, of probability 0, so Xn​→X almost surely (but not surely).

Takeaway. The limiting interval is [0,21​] but X is defined with [0,21​). The mismatch at one endpoint is exactly what "almost" forgives.

B3 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 3). Xn​=±n1​ with probability 21​ each. Show Xn​a.s.​0.

Solution

Solution. Route 2. Whatever the sign, ∣Xn​∣=n1​. So for a fixed ϵ>0,

P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(n1​>ϵ)={10​n<ϵ1​n≥ϵ1​.​

The series ∑n​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ) has at most ⌊ϵ1​⌋ non-zero terms, so it is finite, and Theorem 7.5 gives Xn​a.s.​0.

Takeaway. Here the convergence is even sure: ∣Xn​(ω)∣≤n1​ for every ω, whatever the signs are and however they depend on each other. The randomness in the sign is irrelevant because the size is deterministic.

B4 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 4; last year's HW8 Q1(b)). Xn​ independent, Xn​∼ Bernoulli(n1​). Does Xn​→0 almost surely?

Solution

Solution. The answer is no. Let's see why, and why the easy route fails first.

Route 2 fails. For 0<ϵ<1, P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(Xn​=1)=n1​, and ∑n​n1​=∞. Theorem 7.5 says nothing.

Route 3. Since Xn​∈{0,1}, for 0<ϵ<1 being within ϵ of 0 means being 0. So

Am​={Xn​=0 for all n≥m}.

We cannot compute an infinite product directly, so bound it. For any N≥m, Am​ is contained in the finite event "Xm​=⋯=XN​=0". By independence, the probability of that event is a product:

P(Am​)≤P(Xm​=0,…,XN​=0)=(1−m1​)⋯(1−N1​)=mm−1​⋅m+1m​⋯NN−1​.

The product telescopes: each numerator cancels the previous denominator, leaving Nm−1​. This holds for every N≥m, and Nm−1​→0 as N→∞. So P(Am​)=0 for every m, and

m→∞lim​P(Am​)=0=1.

By Theorem 7.6 there is no almost sure convergence. In fact, with probability 1 the sequence contains infinitely many 1s: whatever m you pick, a 1 appears after time m.

One-line alternative (route 4). The events {Xn​=1} are independent and ∑n1​=∞, so by the second Borel–Cantelli lemma infinitely many of them happen, with probability 1.

Takeaway: compare with slide 19. In both examples P(Xn​=0)=n1​. The marginal laws are the same! The difference is the dependence. On slide 19 the events {U≤n1​} are nested (all driven by one U), so the 1s stop. Here they are independent, so the 1s keep coming back forever. Almost sure convergence depends on the joint behaviour of the sequence, not just the law of each Xn​.

B5 (last year's HW8 Q10 and HW7 Q4). Yn​∼ Bernoulli(n+1n​) independent, and Xn+1​=Y1​Y2​⋯Yn​. Show Xn​a.s.​0 (and hence in probability).

Solution

Solution. Step 1: the probability of a 1. A product of 0s and 1s is 1 only if every factor is 1. By independence,

P(Xn+1​=1)=k=1∏n​P(Yk​=1)=k=1∏n​k+1k​=21​⋅32​⋯n+1n​=n+11​→0.

(Again the product telescopes.) So P(Xn​=1)=n1​.

Step 2: the path is absorbing. Each step multiplies by Yn​∈{0,1}, so the sequence can only stay or drop. Once it hits 0, it is 0 forever. (It looks like 1,1,1,…,1,0,0,0,…)

Step 3: Route 3. Because of absorption, staying at 0 from time m on is the same as being 0 at time m:

Am​={Xn​=0 for all n≥m}={Xm​=0},P(Am​)=1−m1​→1.

By Theorem 7.6, Xn​→0 almost surely.

Equivalent view. The only way to avoid convergence is Yk​=1 for every k. That event is inside {Xn+1​=1} for every n, so its probability is at most n+11​ for every n, hence 0.

Takeaway. Once more ∑n​P(Xn​=1)=∑n1​=∞, so Theorem 7.5 is no help. This is the same situation as slide 19, not B4: the events {Xn​=1} are nested (each one implies all the earlier ones), not independent. Nested events with a divergent sum can still give almost sure convergence.

B6 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 2). X1​,X2​,… i.i.d. U(0,1) and Yn​=min(X1​,…,Xn​). Show Yn​a.s.​0.

Solution

Solution. Route 2. The minimum is above ϵ exactly when every Xi​ is above ϵ (L13's trick for minima). For 0<ϵ<1, by independence,

P(Yn​>ϵ)=P(X1​>ϵ,…,Xn​>ϵ)=(1−ϵ)n.

This is a geometric series with ratio 1−ϵ<1:

n=1∑∞​(1−ϵ)n=ϵ1−ϵ​<∞.

So Theorem 7.5 gives Yn​→0 almost surely. (For ϵ≥1 the probabilities are all 0, so there is nothing to check.)

Takeaway. Geometric decay is always summable. Also note Yn​ is non-increasing, so route 3 would work too: Am​={Ym​<ϵ} (once below ϵ, the minimum stays below), and P(Am​)=1−(1−ϵ)m→1.

B7 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 3). Xn​∼N(0,n1​). Show Xn​a.s.​0.

Solution

Solution. Route 2. First standardize: Xn​ has the same law as n​Z​ with Z∼N(0,1). So

P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(∣Z∣>ϵn​)=2(1−Φ(ϵn​)).

We cannot sum Φ values exactly, so bound them. Use the Gaussian tail bound 1−Φ(x)≤21​e−x2/2 for x≥0, with x=ϵn​, so x2=ϵ2n:

n∑​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤n∑​2⋅21​e−ϵ2n/2=n∑​(e−ϵ2/2)n<∞.

This is a geometric series with ratio e−ϵ2/2<1. Theorem 7.5 gives almost sure convergence.

Takeaway. The problem never said how the Xn​ depend on each other, and it did not need to: Theorem 7.5 never uses independence. Also, Chebyshev alone would only give P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤nϵ21​, whose sum diverges, so you really need the stronger Gaussian tail here.

B8 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 4). On Ω=[0,1] with uniform probability, Xn​(s)=n+1n​s+(1−s)n and X(s)=s. Show Xn​a.s.​X.

Solution

Solution. Route 1. Fix s and take the two terms separately.

  • First term: n+1n​→1, so n+1n​s→s for every s.
  • Second term: (1−s)n. If 0<s≤1 then 0≤1−s<1, so (1−s)n→0 (as in slide 13). If s=0 then (1−s)n=1 for every n.

So for 0<s≤1, Xn​(s)→s+0=s=X(s). ✓ At s=0, Xn​(0)=0+1=1 for all n, so Xn​(0)→1=0=X(0). ✗

The failure set is {0}, which has probability 0, so Xn​a.s.​X.

B9 (Bertsekas Problem 13; last year's Tutorial 8 Q7). (a) If Xn​→a and Yn​→b almost surely, show Xn​+Yn​→a+b almost surely. (b) Find limn→∞​∑i=1n​Xi​∑i=1n​Xi2​​ for i.i.d. Xi​∼U[0,1].

Solution

Solution. (a) The idea: throw away the bad outcomes of both sequences at once; what is left is still probability 1, and on it everything is ordinary real analysis.

  • Let A={Xn​→a} and B={Yn​→b}. Both have probability 0.
  • For any ω outside A∪B, both Xn​(ω)→a and Yn​(ω)→b are ordinary convergent sequences of numbers, so their sum converges to a+b (limit of a sum of real sequences).
  • So the failure set of Xn​+Yn​ is inside A∪B, and P(A∪B)≤P(A)+P(B)=0.

The same argument works for products, for ratios (when b=0), and for any continuous function g: g(Xn​,Yn​)→g(a,b) almost surely. This is the "continuous mapping" property of almost sure convergence.

(b) The trick: a ratio of two sums is a ratio of two averages, because the n1​'s cancel:

∑i=1n​Xi​∑i=1n​Xi2​​=n1​∑i=1n​Xi​n1​∑i=1n​Xi2​​.

Now apply the SLLN twice.

  • Top: the Xi2​ are i.i.d. with mean E[X2]=∫01​x2dx=31​, so n1​∑Xi2​a.s.​31​.
  • Bottom: n1​∑Xi​a.s.​E[X]=21​.

By (a) applied to the ratio g(x,y)=yx​, which is continuous at (31​,21​) since 21​=0:

∑Xi​∑Xi2​​a.s.​1/21/3​=32​.

B10 (Bertsekas Problem 14). Xi​ i.i.d. and Yi​ i.i.d., with finite means and E[Y]=0. Does Zn​=Y1​+⋯+Yn​X1​+⋯+Xn​​ converge almost surely?

Solution

Solution. Yes, by the same trick as B9(b). Divide top and bottom by n:

Zn​=(Y1​+⋯+Yn​)/n(X1​+⋯+Xn​)/n​.

By the SLLN the top tends to E[X] and the bottom to E[Y], almost surely. Since E[Y]=0, the ratio is continuous at the limit, and B9(a) gives

Zn​a.s.​E[Y]E[X]​.

Note. No independence between the two sequences is needed. Each SLLN uses only the i.i.d. property within its own sequence, and B9(a) never needs independence (it only combines two probability-1 events).

B11 (exam-style contrast with slide 19). Let U1​,U2​,… be independent uniforms and Xn​=n21{Un​≤n21​}. Does Xn​→0 almost surely? What is E[Xn​]?

Solution

Solution. Almost sure convergence (route 2). For 0<ϵ<1,

P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(Un​≤n21​)=n21​,n∑​n21​=6π2​<∞.

By Theorem 7.5, Xn​→0 almost surely. This holds even though the Un​ are independent: the bad events are now rare enough that, with probability 1, only finitely many happen.

The means. E[Xn​]=n2⋅P(Un​≤n21​)=n2⋅n21​=1 for every n. So again the means stay at 1 while the limit is 0.

Takeaway: three cases side by side.

set-up P(Xn​=0) a.s. to 0? reason
one U: n1{U≤n1​} (slide 19) n1​ yes nested events (Thm 7.6)
independent Un​: n1{Un​≤n1​} (L18 slide 20) n1​ no independent, ∑n1​=∞ (2nd B–C)
independent Un​: n21{Un​≤n21​} (this) n21​ yes ∑n21​<∞ (Thm 7.5)

In all three, E[Xn​]=1→0.

B12 (Bertsekas Problems 16 and 18, optional): the SLLN with a finite fourth moment. This is the standard short proof. It assumes more than the theorem needs, namely E[Xi4​]<∞, and (after subtracting the mean from every Xi​) E[Xi​]=0, so we must show nSn​​→0.

  1. A criterion (Problem 16). If Yn​≥0 and ∑n​E[Yn​]<∞, then Yn​→0 almost surely. Reason: the Yn​ are non-negative, so we may swap sum and expectation: E[∑n​Yn​]=∑n​E[Yn​]<∞. A random variable with finite mean is finite with probability 1, so ∑n​Yn​<∞ with probability 1. And the terms of a convergent series tend to 0.
  2. The fourth moment of the sum. Expand
E[Sn4​]=E[(i∑​Xi​)4]=i,j,k,l∑​E[Xi​Xj​Xk​Xl​].

Look at which terms survive.

  • If some index appears exactly once, say i differs from j,k,l, then by independence E[Xi​Xj​Xk​Xl​]=E[Xi​]E[Xj​Xk​Xl​]=0.
  • All four equal (i=j=k=l): n terms, each E[X4].
  • Two distinct indices, each appearing twice: choose which of the 3 ways to pair up the four positions ({1,2}{3,4}, {1,3}{2,4}, {1,4}{2,3}), then the two values i=j in order, n(n−1) ways. That is 3n(n−1) terms, each E[Xi2​]E[Xj2​]=(E[X2])2≤E[X4].

So E[Sn4​]≤(n+3n(n−1))E[X4]≤3n2E[X4]. That is, E[Sn4​]≤Cn2 with C=3E[X4] (as in Bertsekas). The point is the growth rate: n2, not the n4 you would get if there were no cancellation. 3. Apply the criterion to Yn​=(nSn​​)4≥0:

n∑​E[Yn​]=n∑​n4E[Sn4​]​≤n∑​n4Cn2​=Cn∑​n21​<∞.

So (nSn​​)4→0 almost surely, and taking fourth roots, nSn​​→0 almost surely. □

Why the fourth power? With the second moment you only get E[(nSn​​)2]=nσ2​, and ∑n1​=∞, so the criterion fails. That route gives only the weak law (L18). The fourth power buys the extra factor of n1​ needed to make the series converge.

The general SLLN (finite mean only) needs a harder proof, which is beyond the course.

B13 (concept check). True or false? (a) If Xn​→X surely then Xn​→X almost surely. (b) If ∑n​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=∞ for some ϵ, then Xn​→0 almost surely. (c) If Xn​a.s.​X then E[Xn​]→E[X].

Answers. (a) True. If every path converges, then C=Ω and P(C)=1. (b) False in general. Slide 19 and B5 are counterexamples: the sum is ∑n1​=∞, yet Xn​→0 almost surely. Theorem 7.5 is only sufficient. The statement becomes true when the events {∣Xn​∣>ϵ} are independent, by the second Borel–Cantelli lemma (as in B4). (c) False. Slide 19: Xn​→0 almost surely but E[Xn​]=1 for all n. The rare huge values ("mass escaping to infinity") keep the mean up.
